https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7: The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93: Between 2013 and 2026, almost 250,000 badgers were killed in England as part of widespread culling to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB)
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers , external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.

This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.
Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".
In July, the Senedd backed a Reform UK motion calling on the Welsh Government to consider targeted wildlife control, including badger culling
Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.
They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.
Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.
There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.
For farming families "a TB breakdown can mean months or years of restrictions, uncertainty and difficult choices", said agriculture minister Llyr Gruffydd
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".
"We will not stand by while farmers face uncertainty and anxiety, nor will we pursue a mass non-selective cull," he added.
"Instead, we will be taking evidence-based and science-led action, incorporating the three pillars of cattle, people and wildlife.
"Farmers and the public will rightly judge us on whether we prevent disease and reduce its impact, even when the decisions are difficult."

Much of the US east coast will experience heavy rain over the holiday

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial , external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy: Australia's Chris Bowen sits at the top table at the summit surrounded by other delegates
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Climate advocates reacted with dismay at the failure of the talks.
Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".
The COP process was "in need of significant reform", Gore wrote on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."
"It's time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world," he added.
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w: After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo has arrived at its final destination and is now in orbit around Mercury.

It‘s operating in an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit was a perilous one: a 37-minute handbrake turn that allowed it to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

The European Space Agency said on X that the probe had made contact and its telemetry data confirmed that it was now flying around the planet, though it's thrusters had fired for a shorter time than planned following a software issue.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq78: Efforts to avert the collapse of talks at the UN COP31 summit have faced further delays on the second day of overtime, as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.

Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
Countries were expected to reconvene to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting was delayed on Sunday morning.
The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday.
But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
The new draft also includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history.

If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.

The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.

As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President Murat Kurum says he believes the third version of the text sent to delegates addresses outlying concerns.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly: Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.
If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.
In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement
On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.

"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."
Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
Beyond this point scientists warn , external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting new global energy demand , outstripping oil and gas , external .

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War continues, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g: Flames engulfed Hudson Valley farm as 200 first responders arrived at the scene
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.

Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Hudson Valley Farms is in a legal battle with the state of New York over its foie gras ban
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.

Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.

Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xg: Switching to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet the UK's net zero targets
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March .
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets .
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.

Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many .

The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.
Check if you are eligible for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme , external
For low-income households and those in social housing, the government is providing an extra £5bn for the Warm Homes Local Grant , external and the Social Housing Fund , external .
Scotland , external and Northern Ireland , external have separate schemes to help make homes more efficient.
UK households can also apply for low and no interest loans of between £7,500 and £35,000 to install green technologies under the Warm Homes Loan Scheme , external .
The government has promised to keep funding for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at £400m in 2027-28 before increasing it in line with inflation.
However, this represents a significant cut compared to what was previously announced.

Some of the money the energy and environment departments have to spend on loans and investments is also being diverted towards the £4.7bn "Your First Home" scheme, which aims to help people purchase a property.
This could mean further cuts to the Warm Homes Scheme, but the government has said it "remains committed to heat-pump deployment".
Heat pump installations currently benefit from a 0% VAT rate, but this is set to rise to 5% in April 2027.

While the upfront costs remain substantial, heat pumps could become cheaper to run than gas boilers, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC) , external , which advises the UK government on cutting emissions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c607: Africa is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn)
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678: Television cook Delia Smith has joined opponents of a £1.2bn data centre, arguing it would threaten a nature reserve.
Campaigners fear the proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.

Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said: "I love Norfolk. You can't be involved in a football club for 55 years without being attached to the people and the beauty of Norfolk. I feel very strongly about it."
But developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.
Delia Smith, pictured with fellow campaigner Jake Humphrey, says she feels very strongly about protecting Norfolk
Data centres are facilities that store and process vast amounts of data and run the software and online services used by millions of people.
This centre, off the A140 Ipswich Road, would need 150 MW of power to run and would feature 72 chiller units on its roof.
According to planning documents, the building would be about 20m (65ft) high.
A planning application for the centre has been lodged with South Norfolk Council.
If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027 and it would be operational by 2028.

The plans have emerged at the same time as a much bigger proposal for a data centre and solar farm elsewhere in Norfolk, south of King's Lynn, which would require more than five times as much electricity.
The developer has said the Keswick facility would use " air-cooling technology " and not require water for cooling.
But Smith, who lives in Suffolk, said: "We haven't got enough water, and data centres use an awful lot of water.

""It's one of the biggest [data centres] and It doesn't do anything for the Norfolk community. Where is the £1.2bn coming from? And who are the people who are going to presumably make money out of it?
"It's not going to do anything for the local community, it's the opposite. It's going to be bad."
Campaigners have raised concerns about the proposed centre's effect on the nearby Marston Marsh nature reserve
It is hoped the centre will harness wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.
Smith said: "Renewable energy is going into the grid but it doesn't supply everything now.
"What are you going to do when you have this huge data centre absolutely sucking up energy?"
Other opponents of the plan include broadcaster and entrepreneur Jake Humphrey .
Matt Tomlinson is worried that nocturnal wildlife including owls and bats will be driven away from the area
Other campaigners include Matt Tomlinson of Yare Valley Meadow Makers, who believes the development will have a "disastrous effect" on nocturnal wildlife.
"On this Marston Marsh site we have nine protected bat species, we have three different owl species and these will all need the quiet conditions to effectively hunt," he said.
"I think this is an awful idea; awful for the wildlife and awful for the people."

In recent days, Labour MP for South Norfolk, Ben Goldsborough, who believes the development would be in the wrong place , has been appointed to a new data centre committee that will scrutinise the government's national policies.

Matt Bartram, chief executive of Norwich Apex, said: "Our ambition is to deliver one of the UK's greenest data centres, using low-carbon power supplied via Norwich Main substation. Protecting nearby ecological sites, including Marston Marshes has shaped the design from the outset.
"Detailed environment assessments have informed our plans to reduce noise and screen the development from view.
"We propose planting more than 15,700 trees and over 1.7km of new hedgerow, with the plans delivering a 13% biodiversity net gain."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr78: Buttermere has been described as a "fragile ecosystem under pressure"
Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.
Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.
A new report has found farming practices alone "cannot account" for the changes.
West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".
The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.
WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".
Buttermere is a naturally nutrient-poor lake, the organisation said, which provides a welcoming environment for sensitive species, such as the Arctic charr cold-water fish.
But algae triggered by excess phosphorus can "choke out these rare habitats and degrade the lake's protected status", WCRT added.

Local wastewater infrastructure was identified as a "key area of concern", the organisation said, while agricultural investigations across major landholdings found no evidence of systemic diffuse pollution or excessive nutrient use, with soil management plans broadly appropriate.
As they are not connected to mains drainage, many properties in the area rely on septic tanks or package treatment plants.

However, WCRT said a number of the 11 septic tank systems identified in the catchment were "undersized, poorly maintained or past their effective lifespan, with several suspected to be discharging directly to surface water, which is not compliant with the regulations".
Although most owners were keen to help the environment, the trust said there was a "widespread lack of awareness" about how the private systems worked and what level of maintenance was needed.
Surveys also revealed just over 40% of visitors had dogs with them and many were walked along sensitive lakeshore paths.
Nutrient fertilisation by the animals "could be significant", it was found.

WCRT CEO Jodie Mills, said: "Our investigations show that water quality in Buttermere is suffering primarily due to private wastewater systems that are undersized, poorly maintained or overwhelmed during peak seasonal surges.
"Many home and business owners simply didn't realise their tanks weren't performing properly.
"This creates a hidden source of pollution, and urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed to protect this special lake."

In addition to calling for regulation and enforcement, the trust said it would be providing wastewater guidance for homeowners on its website and engaging with the local parish council and the Lake District Visitor Management Group, which includes the National Trust and the Lake District National Park Authority.
Responsibility for the regulation of discharges belongs to the EA.
Peter Miles, the organisation's nature, monitoring and technical manager, said the report provided "valuable information about the sources of excess nutrients" in Buttermere.

He added: "Sources of pollution are often very complex and we urge everyone living or working in Buttermere, and those visiting, to play their part in reducing the amount of pollution entering the lake, from checking their private sewage systems to clearing up after their dogs."

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2764606%2Frma-expert-questions-fonterra-s-application-to-dump-22m-litres-of-milk
A resource management expert is questioning Fonterra's rationale in applying for consent to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury.

The dairy giant has applied to the regional council to vary the conditions of seven consents, arguing approval is needed because of a forecast milk surplus due to processing constraints in the South Island.

Fonterra director of NZ Manufacturing Chris Kane told Morning Report the company had the capacity to process the milk , and the dumping would only bever happen if there was a major event like a power cut or a natural disaster.
"We'd only have surplus milk if we couldn't process it, and we couldn't process it because we had a power shortage or we had some other force majeure event," he said.
"It's highly unlikely we'll ever have to use that because we have a network of 24 sites."
There is no mention of a force majeure event in the application to the regional council.
Kane said there was no issue of surplus milk, and the repeated use of the phrase in the company's consent application was a "technicality."
Resource management practitioner Greg Carylon said there were already provisions in the Resource Management Act that allowed for emergency milk dumping from unforeseeable events.
References being made now to the consent being sought in case of a natural disaster seemed to be a "retrospective response," he said.

"They would have had a gap there and would have been trying to close it on a responsible basis, but the reality is they're overproducing at times across a number of plants around the motu and the cost of that is being externalised to the environment and community where it should not be."
"There was all sorts of outcomes from that earthquake that were unanticipated, and it drove all sorts of exercises, emergency road building, sewage discharges into the moana.

"Whatever it might be, there's an avenue for those reasonable, necessary undertakings, but in this case, Fonterra could simply take the steps that it knows it could and provide capacity for overproduction in its own plants in a more responsible way."
Fonterra was able to predict the surge in milk and constraints on processing capacity because it was inevitable, Carylon said.
"[Fonterra] has deliberately designed and built the system that we're seeing now, and it's been occurring over two and a half decades.
"It's easy to anticipate, it's just expensive to resolve and it's obviously from their perspective a lot easier if someone else resolves it at someone else's cost."
He said Fonterra's strategy was once producing boutique products, but it had become a bulk supplier to the world.
"It means that when we're working in bulk, we have these massive peaks that come through, and to process it all into one product at one time is problematic."
Fonterra exports 95 percent of its milk, primarily as milk powder.
Future Farmers spokesperson and contract milker Daniel Judd said he did not think Fonterra would dump milk unless it absolutely had to.
He puts the supply surge down to dairy conversions allowing for tens of thousands more cows on the Canterbury plains in the last two years, and shifts in supply from other milk processors.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/276498: Beef mince that was sold at an Auckland supermarket is being recalled over concerns it may contain small pieces of metal.

A social media creator says overseas online casinos are offering him thousands of dollars to advertise their platforms, even though it's illegal.
With Aotearoa moving to license online casinos , there's concerns operators will keep flouting the law on social media.
Advocates say it's time for tougher advertising restrictions and bigger fines for those who break the rules.

Auckland-based social media content creator Jackson Francis posts photos and videos he's taken of cars and his overseas travels. On his Instagram page he's followed by just under 20,000 people, a large number being men aged between 18 and 21.
From the middle of this year, he said he had been getting weekly messages from overseas-based online casinos, asking him if he would advertise for them.
Checkpoint has seen some of the offers, sent through emails and private messages.
One of the casinos offered him $3500 for 10 Instagram stories. Another sent a script for him to follow and said they would supply video for him to post, so it would appear as though he had won money.
All up, Francis told Checkpoint he's been offered around $35,000.
"It would probably be the easiest money you'd ever get too, you'd just film a quick iPhone video, takes you five minutes then you post it to your story."
But Francis turned the offers down, as he didn't want to sell his followers out.
"It's not worth it, [the online casinos] are just preying on the smaller influencers, the ones out there posting and they don't have hundreds of thousands of followers."
"They're probably the most likely ones to say yes to a quick, easy couple thousand dollars."
Since May last year, nine social media influencers have been given infringement notices by the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA).
Each infringement costs $5000 each, with four influencers slapped with $20,000 worth of fines.
Frances Russell, clinical lead of support service Touchgrass said online gambling has become normalised for young people, through advertising on social media and in sport.
"Seeing it pop up like that can be a real trigger for young brains - you might struggle a little bit with impulse control.
"They might be having a bit of a wobbly day and that can lead them into paths of gambling that they hadn't intended to do, so I don't think that it is harm-free."
Russell said she's seeing teenagers as young as 17 seeking help for problem online gambling.
"What I see with young people is a lot of feelings of shame and guilt around the kind of destruction that it causes in their lives, young people losing quite significant amounts of money.

"I'm also seeing young people who originally started out as having really well-rounded lives, being members of sports teams and going out with friends, [now] making active choices to stay home and gamble, because they're chasing losses."
Problem Gambling Foundation's Andree Froude said despite it being illegal, some social media influencers are still taking up offers because the fines aren't hefty enough.
"For those operators, it's like a cost doing business, it's not really a penalty.
"I know in some situations the operators probably covered the costs of these fines for the influencer."

An Auckland vehicle importer has been jailed for nearly two and a half years for winding back odometers by almost 50 million kilometres.
The man was also ordered to pay $27,000 in reparation, while his company was ordered to pay a further $315,000.

A Customs investigation - in collaboration with the NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi - looked at 174 used vehicles imported from Japan and found the importer had been intentionally winding back odometers between August 2020 and January 2024 to make the vehicles appear more valuable.
In total, 48,674,800 kilometres in mileage was wiped from odometers.
Individual vehicles had between 60,000 and 840,000 kilometres wound back, and Customs estimated the profit was close to $5.6 million.
The imported trucks had rolled-back odometers and forged documents.
Customs acting investigations manager Nigel Barnes said the man's actions were not an error.
"This was deliberate and calculated fraud. The man wound back odometers and forged export certificates to conceal the vehicles' true histories and inflate their value.
"Accurate mileage helps people assess a vehicle's value, safety, and maintenance needs. The deception denied buyers the information they needed to make informed decisions."
Some forged certificates contained false information about their year of manufacture or carrying capacity.
NZTA head of vehicle regulation Geoff Williamson said all affected vehicle owners had been contacted, and those in use were "recalled, corrected, and when required, recertified".

An MP calling for changes to New Zealand's assisted dying law says people should not be forced to leave the country in order to die with dignity.

The ACT Party's Todd Stephenson has drafted a private member's bill which would remove the rule that people could opt for assisted dying only if they were terminally ill and had six months or less to live.
The bill would have to be drawn from the parliamentary ballot before it could be debated by MPs and have any chance of becoming law.
However, opponents of a law change say broadening the criteria could put disabled people at serious risk.
They fear disabled people could ask for assisted dying not because they wanted to end their lives, but because they could not get the support, housing and care they needed.

Criticism of New Zealand's existing End of Life Choice Act - too restrictive for some, a moral anathema to others - is back in the spotlight after a 93-year-old woman had to travel overseas to fulfil her wish of assisted dying.
Brothers Justin and Peter Topzand said they took their mother Margaret to Switzerland so she could end her life on her own terms, rather than suffer a long, slow decline into dementia and dependence.
Margaret Topzand, seen here with son Peter, enjoying the sun during one of her last walks in the Swiss countryside.
They said she was not eligible for assisted dying in New Zealand because she was not expected to die within six months from a terminal illness.

Justin Topzand said it was "ridiculous" the current law forced people to travel halfway across the planet for a medically simple procedure; while Peter Topzand said it was "appalling" people who could not afford to travel to Switzerland were unable to access assisted dying.
The End of Life Choice Act started as a private member's bill introduced by ACT leader David Seymour in 2017.
It became law in 2021 after passing a conscience vote in Parliament and gaining roughly two-to-one support in a referendum held alongside the 2020 general election.
Act MP Todd Stephenson said his party was proud of getting an assisted dying law across the line, but many people were still missing out.
"I've heard from many, many New Zealanders who have loved ones who are sick and who want to access the end-of-life choice regime, but unfortunately, they are still not eligible."
Stephenson said his bill, if passed, would adopt all 25 recommendations made in a health ministry review of the existing law.
More importantly, he said, it would remove the "arbitrary" six-month rule.

"We think people being able to make decisions around how they die - and having that dignity at the end of their life - is really, really important. It's not an option for everyone. It's actually people's individual decisions about whether they apply," he said.
"But when they're living with a terminal illness, we want them to have that option so they don't have to leave New Zealand and seek other ways of getting assisted dying."
Disabled Persons Assembly chief executive and former Green MP Mojo Mathers has grave concerns about what an expanded assisted dying law could mean for disabled people.

The head of New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre says AI is accelerating the speed and scale of cyber threats after several Allied Media newspapers - including the Otago Daily Times - were affected by an attack.
Catriona Robinson, who is also the deputy director of General Cyber Security, told Checkpoint AI tools intended to help check for cyber vulnerabilities were now being used to conduct cyber attacks.

"So these tools were available on a public repository... They're being repurposed by cyber criminals, and that's accelerating the pace and scale at which those criminals are able to launch cyber attacks."
This comes after Allied Media confirmed on Tuesday it had been the target of an attack that had "disrupted several of our production systems".
It said community papers that were due out on Wednesday - including the Blenheim Sun, Southern Rural Life and The Ensign - will now be delivered on Thursday.
"Our teams are working to restore access to our systems so that we can produce tomorrow's Otago Daily Times."
Greymouth Star's deputy editor Brendon McMahon confirmed today' edition could not be published and Wednesday's Hokitika Guardian could also not go ahead.
"The internet issue has impacted the entire Allied Media group South Island-wide..." McMahon said
"We hope to provide an update later in the day on the timing to solve what is a complex issue , and hopefully tomorrow will be a new day!"
He thanked readers for their patience. Allied Media said there was no evidence that customer information had been accessed.
More recently Top Ten Holiday Parks Group said it was hacked, leading to phishing scams that targeted guests.
Last week, the Defence Force shut down some of its public websites after a cyber attack and Forrest and Bird also confirmed it had been hacked.
Robinson said the National Cyber Security Centre was helping these organisations deal with the attacks, which don't appear to be linked.
She said attacks were on the rise and the centre had seen the highest quarterly total of cyber incidents being reported in two years.
"We're talking about 1700... It concerns me a great deal, you know, that the environment is getting more turbulent."
The centre was working with critical infrastructure companies in New Zealand to help them prepare, including those in telecommunication and finance.
A cyber criminals motivation was financial, Robinson said, and they tend to go for sectors rich in sensitive and personal information.
"On the dark web, you can absolutely purchase a cyber criminal service to go and steal information for you... which you can then launch attacks against other organisations with."
She also said it was highlighted in their recent cyber threat report that international state actors were another documented threat, including those from China, Russia and Iran.

"We assess that China is the most persistent and capable state sponsored actor acting against New Zealand... when we see state sponsored activity in New Zealand, it seems predominantly to be aimed at espionage purposes and other forms of information theft, intellectual property theft, for example."
Robinson said there was one case with a North Korean IT worker scamming their way into a role with a major New Zealand company and putting it at risk of breaching sanctions legislation.

Nelson City Council has held an emergency behind-closed-doors meeting following a falling-out between the chief executive and mayor.

Tuesday's meeting was called at the urging of the Chief Executive Employment Committee to discuss a confidential complaint process as the committee said the matter had to be dealt with and could not be delayed.
Council staff said the complaint was a confidential matter and they could not share any details about it.
The extraordinary meeting comes after concerns were raised about Mayor Nick Smith's behaviour towards chief executive Nigel Philpott, councillors and staff.

Smith confirmed to RNZ a code of conduct complaint was made against him in July after a closed-door meeting a month earlier when elected members debated whether to remove first-term councillor Lisa Austin from office over her business interests.
Austin said a code of conduct complaint had also been made against her over the same issue.
Austin and her husband own Austin Transport Tippers Ltd that supplies trucks to two council contractors for haulage work but does not have any direct contracts with Nelson City Council.

The law prevents people from being elected or appointed as a member of a council if they have contracts or subcontracts from the council totalling more than $100,000 per year unless the auditor-general grants an exemption. The amount was previously $25,000 but was increased on 6 June.
Elected members voted to let Austin remain on council and not proceed with a by-election.
Smith told RNZ there was an argument with raised voices between himself and Philpott over the decision not to disclose how councillors voted at the June meeting.
The mayor requested members' votes were recorded but alleged Philpott said the votes should remain anonymous so those voting to remove Austin were not subject to criticism.
Smith said he was put under "enormous pressure" to agree for the vote to be kept secret and the complainants alleged he intimidated councillors by saying the vote would be made public.
Code of conduct complaints were costing ratepayers tens of thousands of dollars and were "a huge distraction for Council getting on with the job for the people of Nelson", he said.
He was disappointed details of the code of conduct had been leaked to media and, while he respected the confidentiality of the process, he would continue to defend himself, Smith said.
Philpott said there was a confidential process that needed to be followed and it was unfortunate the matter was in the public arena.
"To protect the integrity of this process, I have reminded all elected members and senior staff that it should be treated confidentially at this stage, without exception.
"It would be inappropriate for me to comment further at this time."
Councillors RNZ spoke to did not want to comment on the code of conduct complaint.
Deputy Mayor Pete Rainey said the process was confidential, and commenting on it was "inexcusable".

"There's a bit of an unwritten rule as far as councils are concerned, in my experience, is that when council makes a decision, once a decision is made, it should be supported by elected members, whether you agree with the decision or not."

Austin previously told RNZ she had worked with lawyer Dr Mai Chen to ensure the council and the Audit Office had correct information and confirmed she was legally allowed to stand for election and be elected as a councillor.

Smith said the issue of Austin's eligibility to be a councillor should have ended in May, when the Audit Office decided it was not in the public interest to prosecute her and he was defending the democratic process by which she was elected.

Council documents show at least three other places where speed signs went up near Queenstown before the new limits were legally enforceable.

There was also a 60km/h electronic variable speed limit used at the base of Cardrona Ski Field Road that was yet to be legalised.

Grant Routen wanted to watch the sun rise at his local beach.
The early riser was spending his morning at Te Atatū's Harbour View Beach Reserve when he was greeted by a less than pleasant view.
"I saw something was down here, thinking it was cardboard boxes or something like that," he said.
Routen, who often took it upon himself to clear litter from the reserve, went to take a closer look.
"I would say they were dumped last night. They were completely skinned and the bones were cleaned very well, and they just left the two carcasses, no heads."
The carcasses were largely unidentifiable, save a handful of features.
"[And] on closer examination, one did appear to be a dog. I'm not 100 percent sure, but it certainly looks at points like it's a dog."
"The ears looked far too close together [to be a goat] and they looked exactly like an Alsatian."
"This has happened before, a similar thing, there were entrails and a carcass of some sort. Often, you'll find dumped seafood, but when it's animals like this it's a bit more disturbing."
Routen said he immediately notified Auckland Council, and later contacted police and the SPCA.
"The reaction is pretty bad, there's a lot of outcry. People are just disturbed that this is happening," he said.
"I feel physically sick," one commenter said. "What sort of human does this?"
Routen said he was most disturbed that the carcasses had been dumped in public view.
"It's just not a nice thing for people to see. There are better ways to dispose of this sort of thing... Dig a hole," he said.

"It doesn't need to be thrown out in the public's view, it can be buried. It's great for the garden, it's good fertiliser. It's sad to see they're not taking any consideration for people who see that. It can be traumatic as."
RNZ has approached Auckland Council, police and the SPCA, which are yet to respond.

A Māori researcher is looking at how cultural practices like kapa haka could help support Māori health, as Aotearoa marks Diabetes Action Month this November.

Lincoln University lecturer Dr Hoani Smith (Kāti Mamoe, Kāi Tahu) said kapa haka can support several dimensions of Māori hauora, bringing together physical activity, cultural connection and whanaungatanga.

Smith is one of four researchers to receive funding through the Diabetes New Zealand Research Foundation's 2026 Small Research Grants. Smith's project, Kapa Haka for Metabolic Hauora: A Māori-Led Feasibility Study for Type 2 Diabetes Prevention, will explore how regular participation in kapa haka could support metabolic health and type 2 diabetes prevention .
Māori and Pasifika communities continue to carry a disproportionate burden of health inequities, including type 2 diabetes .
"Kapa haka is something that already exists in our whānau," Smith told RNZ.
"It's deeply embedded in our culture and it's much more than just movement. It's whakapapa, identity, whanaungatanga."
"And we can all strive to be better by doing something that our whānau are enjoying, rather than force it in our communities."
Dr Hoani Smith told RNZ kapa haka is also an opportunity to support physical activity, strengthen connections between generations, and improve overall hauora.
Smith, who specialises in sport, exercise and health research, said a lot of whānau, when they get told what to do without any buy-in, tend not to stick to it .
"And so those habits end up kind of on the wayside after that 21-day cycle.
"So if we can prescribe something that's already been done and we can connect with our people and our culture, it's a win-win for everyone.

"And it also would save long-term down the track inequities that currently exist, because Māori and Pasifika, we carry the heaviest burden. And if we can do something that already exists, mean Māori mean."
Smith draws on the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga - or guardianship - which was announced as this years most beautiful word by international language learning app Babbel.
"So now all of the 'tanga's' can be incorporated and connected to your community ."
He said the physical demands of kapa haka were something he wanted to explore further, alongside the social and cultural connections that came with participating.

"When you actually go to kapa haka practice, they're doing HIIT. They're doing high-intensity training, followed up by waiata, followed up by movements, followed up by playing guitar and then connecting with one another.
"And it goes for many hours. It's not just necessarily go to the gym and exercise for 30, 40 minutes. You're physically and mentally active.
"And the meanest thing is that while singing waiata, you're fatigued as well as having to maintain posture. So it's something rare that I don't think has been researched that well."

Smith said the benefits of kapa haka go beyond just physical health. Haka practices can bring together people of different ages, allowing them to learn from one another while strengthening their connections to their whānau and communities, which he said has an important role to play in supporting the different dimensions of hauora.
"I can be with my elders as well as my grandkids can be with my elders, all at the same time, learning together."
Varron Armstrong steals the show with Ōtiria Marae Kapa Haka.
Using the te ao Māori view of health and wellbeing, Te Whare Tapa Whā, Smith said kapa haka could contribute to several aspects of a person's health, strengthening all pillars.

"The size of the delegation reflects the weight both governments are placing on the visit," In-depth Solomons report said.

An Otago swim club is worried children will miss out on swimming lessons if Dunedin City Council closes their local pool.

The council will consider three options for Port Chalmers Pool at a meeting on Wednesday - closing the pool after the summer season, a new pool key access-only system or keeping the pool open under the existing arrangements with lifeguards.
A staff report said the pool, which was open from September to March, had an approved operating budget of almost $380,000 for the 2026/27 season with expected revenue of about $19,000.
The report said the pool received 4735 visits on average per year, with the net operating cost amounting to $102.73 per visit.
Port Chalmers Swim Club co-president Lisa Dick challenged those figures, saying there were more than 4800 lessons for school children alone and that did not taken into account any public swimming.
Swiping her family season pass counted for one visit, despite having seven people on the pass, she said.
About 100 children per year would miss out on lessons through the swim club if the pool closed, she said.
Dick had hoped to tell the councillors at the meeting about what the community stood to lose if the pool was closed, but said she was not permitted to speak during the public forum.
Council chief executive Richard Briggs said bids to speak about the items relating to the Long Term Plan were being declined, but comprehensive public consultation would start next year.
"We encourage the community to take part when consultation opens, helping shape the priorities, services and investments that will guide Dunedin's future over the next decade," he said.
Dunedin North Intermediate principal Heidi Hayward said it made no sense to limit people's access to pools and swimming lessons.
"Yes, there's a cost factor to it, but there's also a cost factor to people drowning," she said.
"Surely we need to be looking at water safety as a community right and not a privilege."
Dick believed it would be short-sighted to make a decision without speaking to the community.
"People are really upset about this and horrified that we haven't been consulted," she said.
"A decision now could have an impact for generations to come and I just really hope the council takes a breath and considers what those impacts would be."
Dick described the pool as a vital part of the community where children learned to swim, people kept active and spent time with their family and friends.
"You can't undervalue a swimming pool in terms of what it does for communities," she said.
Dick said she had no idea the pool's future was being discussed at the council meeting, until someone alerted her to the agenda item.
She did not think it would be safe to keep the pool open without lifeguards.
Dick's 13-year-old son Freddie learned to swim at the pool and visited at least once a week.
He said it was a beloved part of Port Chalmers and a great place to hang out on a hot day.
"I just love this pool and it would be a shame to see it go and see what it would be turned into. I wouldn't like to see that."
The city council said staff wrote the report following a request from councillors.
"The options remain proposals only and it will be up to council to decide next steps," the council said.
"Depending on their decision, the outcome will then form part of the Long Term Plan public consultation.
"Staff also spoke to the West Harbour Community Board chair about the report prior to its publication."
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/air-nz-br: Air New Zealand is flying long-haul routes from Christchurch again, after a non-stop flight to Singapore took off on 28 October 2026. Long-haul flights are very long trips, often across oceans. Since 2020, the airline had flown very few of them from Christchurch.
More routes are on the way. Direct flights to Tokyo in Japan start on 28 November, and flights to Perth in Australia start on 30 November. A seasonal service to Bali is planned for winter 2027.

Christchurch Airport is expecting its busiest international summer yet, with 21 percent more international seats than before. That’s roughly one extra seat for every five. Even so, Auckland still handles nearly three times as many passengers.

Will smaller towns benefit? Christchurch is also a hub, or meeting point, for flights to smaller places like Queenstown, Dunedin, Nelson, Hokitika and Invercargill. Ajai Jayathilakan, an aviation lecturer at Massey University, warns that these regional communities could miss out.

Figures from NZ Airports looked at routes where another airline, Jetstar, doesn’t compete with Air NZ. On those routes, fares rose 4.2 percent and seat numbers dropped by the same amount. Billie Moore, who led NZ Airports at the time, said, “Regional New Zealand is living the reality of this every day.”
Jayathilakan says the new flights are good news for the South Island. He says ideas like better-linked flight timetables could help smaller towns share in the benefits.

The car has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in California, and the auction takes place in Gardena on Tuesday.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/world-lea: Leaders and scientists from around the world have been meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for a huge United Nations climate conference called COP31 – but talks on an important part of the deal have hit a wall.

Climate scientist Dr Bill Hare, who helps write major international climate reports, said talks about climate finance – money that richer countries give to help poorer countries deal with climate change – are “totally blocked right now.”

“One of the biggest worries at this COP is that there has not been, essentially, the big plan about it,” he said. He wants wealthy countries to triple the money they give to help vulnerable nations adapt to a warmer world, such as by protecting homes from floods and storms.

Dr Hare also pointed out that a small number of countries have been blocking funding and cooperation for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the group of scientists that reviews climate research for the whole world.

On a more positive note, Dr Hare welcomed strong wording in the draft agreement about moving away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas, towards cleaner energy. He said it might be tricky to keep that wording in the final agreement, but he hoped it would survive.
Talks at COP31 are expected to continue as leaders try to find common ground before the summit wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/niue-ocea: A project protecting the ocean around the small Pacific nation of Niue has won one of the world’s most prestigious environmental prizes.

Prince William and Princess Catherine attended the ceremony, along with former New Zealand Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern and Niue’s Prime Minister, Dalton Tagelagi.

In a Facebook post, the trust said the win belonged to the people of Niue.
Niue is aiming to raise $32 million in total to protect and manage its huge ocean area. Winning the Earthshot Prize has now pushed them over the halfway mark towards that goal.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/scientist: For the first time ever, scientists might have directly watched one star swallow up a smaller star right next to it, in a galaxy far, far away.
The giant star, nicknamed “Bao,” is a red giant about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. It is seven times heavier than our sun, and a huge 350 times wider.

Scientists first noticed the star getting brighter back in 2018. By 2023, using special telescopes in the United States, they could see it was definitely growing more luminous. Then, near the end of 2025, they spotted a massive eruption of light coming from the star.

NASA’s powerful James Webb Space Telescope studied the star just 47 days after that eruption, giving scientists important clues. They believe a smaller companion star, about 70 percent as heavy as our sun, spiralled into the giant star’s centre, causing a huge explosion.
“Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult,” said lead scientist Viraj Karambelkar, from Columbia University in the United States.
“When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle, like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean,” he said. “I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this.”
Karambelkar said the discovery proves something scientists had only guessed at before. “I can’t wait to find more,” he said.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/historic-: A carved Māori meeting house that sheltered 50 people during a volcanic eruption almost 140 years ago is finally coming home to Rotorua.
The wharenui (meeting house) is called Hinemihi. She sheltered dozens of people when Mt Tarawera erupted in 1886, one of New Zealand’s most powerful eruptions.

Six years after the eruption, the departing British Governor, William Hillier Onslow, bought Hinemihi and shipped her all the way to his family home in the United Kingdom. She has stood there ever since.

Now, after years of asking, Ngāti Hinemihi will finally get their wharenui back. Officials from the UK’s National Trust and British Council met with Heritage New Zealand and Ngāti Hinemihi in Auckland this week to plan the journey home.
“As long as you’ve got that whare, as long as you’ve got Hinemihi, you’ve got us as well, because we belong to that house,” said Jim Schuster, of Ngāti Hinemihi.
The National Trust has confirmed Hinemihi will be back by 2028, although it still isn’t decided whether she will travel home by air or by sea.
“It is taking a long time, but it’s right to do it well and do it properly,” said Natasha Woollard, of the National Trust.
To thank the UK for looking after Hinemihi so well, Ngāti Hinemihi are gifting new carvings, carrying on the work of her original carver, Tene Waitere.
